normalized_transcript.title: Senior Distributed Systems Engineer (Fintech)
normalized_transcript.job_description: Architecting high-throughput low-latency microservices with Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, and distributed concurrency controls.
normalized_transcript.resume_text: 5+ years backend engineering, distributed caching, event streams.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Welcome Alex. Could you start by introducing yourself and a recent distributed system you architected?

segments.speaker: candidate
segments.text: Thanks! In my last role at Fintech Corp, I led the redesign of our order processing engine handling 15,000 requests per second. We migrated from a monolithic PostgreSQL setup to an event-driven architecture using Kafka and Redis caching.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Interesting. How did you structure the caching layer with Redis to avoid stale reads?

segments.speaker: candidate
segments.text: We implemented a write-through cache pattern with explicit TTL invalidation. When updates occurred, we published an event to Kafka, and worker consumers invalidated corresponding Redis cache keys across cluster nodes.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: What happens when two concurrent transactions try to reserve the same inventory item at the exact same millisecond?

segments.speaker: candidate
segments.text: Uh, like, basically we would just check if the stock is greater than zero in the database, and if so, decrement it. Um, you know, we didn't see many collisions in testing.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Can you elaborate on how you would prevent race conditions without row lock contention?

segments.speaker: candidate
segments.text: Um, maybe we could retry if the write fails or use a queue to serialize all inventory writes.
